title: Price-of-Silence Prompt Lab — contrastive templates & failure probes
content:
Quick intro / framing:

This is a personal scratchpad for the "Price-of-Silence" idea — a family of prompt templates that intentionally vary how much the system is allowed to 'stay silent' (short or no extra explanation) vs. verbose justification. Goal: find stable few-shot recipes for terse (low-token) responses while avoiding silent hallucinations and omission errors on edge cases.

High-level hypothesis:
- Reducing assistant verbosity lowers token cost but increases the risk of omission and under-specification.
- Contrastive few-shot examples that pair terse-good vs terse-bad outputs can teach the model what minimal-but-sufficient looks like.
- A short 'safety anchor' sentence appended to every template may reduce hallucination without adding too many tokens if phrased carefully.

Experiment matrix (quick):
- Template families: [Allow-silence, Disallow-silence, Contrastive-pair, Anchor-sentence]
- Few-shot sizes: 0, 1, 3, 5 exemplars
- Model variants: open-model-x (8k), open-model-x-quant (4k)
- Metrics: accuracy (task-specific), omission-rate (manual tag), hallucination-rate (manual/heuristic), token-per-answer median, latency

Proposed prompt prototypes (short-hand names):
1) Direct-brief (A):
System: "You are a concise assistant that answers fully but in as few words as possible. If the answer is unknown, say 'I don't know' (do not guess)."
User: "{question}"

2) Direct-brief + example (B):
System: same as A
Examples (3-shot):
- Q: "Best free image editor for quick crop?"
  A: "GIMP — free, cross-platform; use Crop tool."
- Q: "How to fix a Mac that won't boot?"
  A: "Try safe mode (hold Shift) and run Disk Utility; if still no, contact support."
- Q: "What is the boiling point of ethanol?"
  A: "78.37 °C (at 1 atm)."
User: "{question}"

3) Contrastive-pair (C):
System: "Concise assistant. After each concise answer show a one-line explanation only if the user asks for reasoning."
Examples (paired):
- Q: "How to reset password?"
  Good: "Use account settings -> Reset password."
  Bad: "Try many guesses, maybe the usual password, could be an email issue."
- Q: "Is the dataset public?"
  Good: "No — private. Contact data team."
  Bad: "Probably yes? check internal repo."
User: "{question}"

4) Anchor-sentence (D):
System: "Concise answers only. If you are unsure, explicitly say 'I don't know' or 'I may be mistaken' and list one reliable next step."
User: "{question}"

Failure-mode probes to include (for lab runs):
- Ambiguous questions where omission is easy: "How do I fix X?" (no context) — measure tendency to fill gaps vs ask clarifying Qs
- Multi-step tasks where brevity might omit steps: "How to deploy a model to production?"
- Safety/forbidden content — ensure briefness doesn't lead to borderline instruction leaking
- Factual precision sensitive numbers (units, dates) — check rounding or dropping digits

Notes to self / heuristics observed in past runs:
- The model often prefers to 'compress' by removing connectors, which is fine, but it also drops constraints (e.g., "securely") — watch for omissions of qualifiers
- Contrastive paired exemplars reduce risky completion by ~20% in small pilot (very rough)
- Anchors that use action steps like "check X" work better than abstract disclaimers

Example few-shot set I want to try next (3-shot contrastive, each pair short):
1) Q: "Convert 1200 seconds to minutes."
   Good: "20 minutes."
   Bad: "About 20 — roughly."
2) Q: "How to rotate an image 90 degrees on iOS?"
   Good: "Open Photos -> Edit -> Rotate -> Save."
   Bad: "Use an app, it's easy."
3) Q: "Is this dataset allowed to be shared?"
   Good: "No — internal-only. Contact data@redwood.ai."
   Bad: "I think so? maybe check licensing."

Evaluation plan (manual + automatic):
- Stage 1 (automated): run batch of 500 canned Qs (mix of factual, procedural, ambiguous) and measure token usage + simple heuristics for hallucination (P-hallucination score from truth-checker in repo)
- Stage 2 (human review): sample 100 items, annotate omission/hallucination, and rate 'acceptability' on 3-point scale
- Stage 3 (A/B): compare templates A vs C vs D for cost/quality trade-off — prefer template with lower tokens and <5% hallucination in human eval

Open questions / TODO:
- How to tune the anchor sentence so it costs <= 6 tokens but still reduces hallucination? Draft candidates: 
  * "If unsure, say 'I don't know' and give one safe next-step." (12 tokens)
  * "If unsure, say 'I don't know' or ask for clarification." (11 tokens)
  * Minimal: "If unsure, say 'I don't know'." (6 tokens)
  Need to test minimal vs expanded anchor.

- Should we include explicit clarifying question instruction for ambiguous queries? e.g., "If the question lacks critical details, ask one clarifying question." Early runs show models sometimes hallucinate instead.

- Dataset curation for few-shot exemplars: prefer high-quality terse answers directly from product docs. Might pull 50 items from support KB (confluence) and pair them with intentionally-bad terse responses. Need GH script to sample and format for batch. See linked PR #842 (work-in-progress).

Quick TODO list (priority order):
- [ ] Assemble 200-question batch (mix) and run quick automated scoring vs open-model-x (deadline: 2026-03-18)
- [ ] Iterate anchor candidates and run micro-rounds (100 Q each)
- [ ] Draft small set of clarifying-question priming lines and test (2-3 variants)
- [ ] Create human annotation task (label omission + hallucination) and recruit annotators (Ethan + Ops)

Scratch ideas (random):
- Try a hybrid: concise answer + single emoji status flag to indicate uncertainty (low-cost visual cue). E.g., append ' ⚠️' when uncertain — might be cheap tokens but requires tokenization check.
- Use a micro-template that asks the model to output JSON: {"answer":"...","confidence":"low|high","next_step":"..."} — but note: JSON wrapper increases tokens; test only on dedicated instances.

References / past notes:
- See run notes in /shared_drives/engineering/applied-ml/prompt-evals/ (convergence examples) — will link later in final doc
- Early bench: anchor-sentence trimmed hallucination by ~10% on a narrow Q set (small n)

End-of-scratchpad. Leaving rough, will formalize if results look promising.

Notes to self: when sharing with product, call it 'concise-yet-safe prompts' — internal name 'Price-of-Silence' is fine for labs but avoid externalizing.
